title: Bilingual Flexibility: The Neurocognitive Basis of Language Control and Adaptation
summary:
Background
People who speak more than one language use both languages very often in everyday life, and their brain has to manage which language to use at any given moment. This constant switching between languages, and the way word meanings can shift depending on experience, are not yet fully understood, especially when it comes to how the brain supports this flexibility.

Research question
This study asks two main questions. First, how does the brain help a bilingual person choose the right language and switch between languages smoothly, especially when the situation calls for quick or planned changes? Second, if a person learns a slightly different meaning for a word while using one language, does this new understanding carry over when they use their other language?

Methodology
Participants take part in tasks where they either say the name of simple pictures out loud in different languages, or judge whether sentences correctly describe the pictures. Some of these tasks are done sitting at a computer, while others are done while lying inside a brain scanner that uses magnetic fields to measure brain activity and brain structure. This allows us to see which parts of the brain are active during these language tasks, and how different brain regions work together. Participation involves one or two separate visits, each lasting about one to two hours, depending on the specific task.
conditions: Healthy adults, no medical condition under investigation. Basic research study on bilingual language control and conceptual adaptation in neurotypical bilingual speakers.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Right-handedness. Neurotypical adults, no known neurological or psychiatric conditions. Normal or corrected to normal vision and hearing. Native language German (L1), English as a second language (L2). For the N-2 repetition-cost experiments (Experiment A3, Workpackage A), participants must additionally speak French as a third language (L3). For all fMRI experiments (Experiments A2 and A4, Workpackage A; Experiment B3, Workpackage B), participants must meet the MRI safety checklist criteria of the Brain Imaging Facility at Uniklinik RWTH Aachen.
Exclusion criteria:
Left-handedness. Known neurological or psychiatric conditions. Uncorrected impairment of vision or hearing. Not a native German speaker, or insufficient proficiency in English as a second language. For Experiment A3 (Workpackage A), insufficient proficiency in French as a third language. For all fMRI experiments (Experiments A2 and A4, Workpackage A; Experiment B3, Workpackage B), any contraindication listed in the MRI safety checklist of the Brain Imaging Facility at Uniklinik RWTH Aachen.
